slides.title: What is a Shear Flow?
slides.text:
What is a Shear Flow?

Definition: adjacent fluid layers moving parallel to each other with different speeds. 


Scenario on the right:
Flow carrying tracer downstream through advection
Tracer spreads and blurs through diffusion
The two fluid layers at the side of the 'white stream' moves at different velocity, hence stretches the tracer

slides.title: What is a Shear Flow?
slides.text:
What is a Shear Flow?

Viscosity:  measure of a fluid's internal resistance to a flow, can be thought of as thickness
 µ
Shear Rate: The rate at which the fluid is deformed (or difference in velocity) due to shear stress
du/dy
Shear Stress: force per unit area exerted (parallel) to a surface by a fluid, causing layers to slide past each other.
𝞽 = µ x du/dy 
(Shear Stress for fluids)

slides.title: Real-World Shear Flow Fluid Dynamics
slides.text:
Real-World Shear Flow Fluid Dynamics

Crude oil pipeline:  
Scenario:  As a fluid moves through a pipe, friction at the pipeline’s walls slows the flow and pressure steadily drops. Especially often with cold, high-viscosity fluids or rough pipes.

Application: Predicting velocity and pressure for different pipeline scenarios, evaluating effectiveness of Drag-Reducing Agents (DRAs)

Advantages: fast and data-driven forecasts


High shear stress required due to friction -> more pump power needed to maintain flow

Pressure falls along the pipeline with accumulating friction   -> less throughput

slides.title: Real-World Shear Flow Fluid Dynamics (in General)
slides.text:
Real-World Shear Flow Fluid Dynamics (in General)

Scenarios of where Shear Flow occurs:  
Industrial pipelines: Oil, gas, and water transportation through pipes
Boundary Layers: Air flowing over airplane wings or car bodies
Natural Environments: ocean currents, river shear zones
Lubrication: Thin oil films in engines and machinery

slides.title: Modeling Objectives
slides.text:
Modeling Objectives

To predict tracer, pressure, and velocity fields in the shear flow system

slides.title: How it motivates the project?
slides.text:
How it motivates the project?

Shear flows driven by pressure exhibit tightly linked advection, viscous diffusion, and pressure effects across fluid layers.

This project aims to utilize deep learning to:
Predict complex fluid dynamics in a more time-efficient, data-driven way
Anticipate transport and flow patterns in biological, environmental, and industrial shear flow systems 
Design better pipelines or industrial fluid systems with the knowledge of shear flow behavior

slides.title: What are we predicting with PARC?
slides.text:
What are we predicting with PARC?

Velocity fields:
 u(x, y, t) and v(x, y, t) – a vector field consisting of horizontal velocity (carries shear layers), and vertical velocity (carries blob perturbations)

Tracer:
s(x, y, t) – a scalar field carried by the flow, indicating the location and the speed of particle diffusion

Pressure Field:
p(x, y, t) – a scalar field that enforces incompressibility and governs the shear flow system

slides.title: Model Building Changes
slides.text:
Model Building Changes

Adjusted Differentiator to take in Reynolds and Schmidt constants fields and consider their time-derivatives as zeroes 
Ensure model learns the real physical dynamics of shear flow

Extracted Single Trajectories for faster training/validation purposes

Adjusted Integrator to take in velocity fields as state variables to ensure model learns velocity evolving in time

slides.title: Model Building Changes
slides.text:
Model Building Changes

Computed spatial reductions & temporal skips for faster and more time-efficient trainings 
Reduced spatial size of data to 1/3 
Skips 10 – 20 temporal steps
Does not undermine the training output

slides.title: Training Strategies #1
slides.text:
Training Strategies #1 

Extract two files {Sc=0.5 & 2.0} for both training and validation

Train on full trajectories and validate on single trajectory samples

Compute validation loss at each epoch, select the model with the lowest loss for final inference

Train two models with different integrators at the same time to evaluate performance

slides.title: Training Strategies #2 (Current)
slides.text:
Training Strategies #2 (Current) 

Extract two files {Sc=0.5 & 2.0} for validation and all files for training

Train and validate on single trajectory samples

Compute validation loss at each epoch, select the model with the lowest loss for final inference

Train two models with different integrators at the same time to evaluate performance

Optimization Results so far

Training time accelerated from 8+ hours per training sample w/ full trajectory -> 6.75 minutes per training sample w/ full trajectory.

Reduced rollout inference MSE on training sample from ~0.12 to ~0.0228 (by ~81%)

slides.title: Trajectory Analysis
slides.text:
Trajectory Analysis

Based on the information from the header file, we know that there are 4 trajectories for each file – we want to compare these to each other across 3 files (at random)
Min/Max Absolute Difference: For each field, we take the trajectories and compute the min & max absolute difference – smallest and largest of those values are the min & max absolute differences
Why does this good? – Catches any change, anywhere, tells us how similar or not (min & max) the runs are to each other
At least 1 identical: min = 0
Every Pair Diff: min > 0 or max >0
All the Same: max = 0
Conclusion: 
Within files: we have four independent starting points randomized by tracer blobs – same scenario slightly tweaked
Amongst files: the files differ in terms of flow regime (different Re & Sc), but the way randomization of the blobs occur does not change
